title: The Wobbly Puppet Problem
markdown:
Even the most earnest of friends can face a puzzle. And so it was with young Zuri and her dear companion, Bloop, a robot of great cheer.

They had a puppet for the Willow Creek Science Fair. This puppet, with colours as bright as a summer meadow, simply refused to stand. It flopped like a wilting flower, its cheerful face bowing towards the dusty ground with a quiet thump. A painted smile looked at the floorboards as if the floorboards were the audience. Zuri and Bloop tried nudging its knees and propping its arms, but still it tumbled, once into a paint pot and once, more politely, against Bloop’s shiny knee. Zuri’s shoulders sagged. The feeling was rather prickly. Bloop nudged the puppet again, and with a comical wobble, it tipped sideways.

Then, into their workshop ambled Coach Ellis. “Ah, a structural challenge!” he boomed gently. He showed Zuri his own arm, a ruler tied to it with string. “My arm has bones inside for shape,” he said. “And then there are muscles, like this string, that pull on the bones to make me move. They work together.” Zuri watched, her eyes wide, as the ruler stayed steady and the string made it bend and straighten. Bloop tilted his head, his lights blinking thoughtfully.

Suddenly Zuri clapped her hands. “Bones and muscles! That’s what our puppet needs!” And so, with newfound energy, Zuri and Bloop gathered cardboard tubes, their puppet’s bones, and stretchy elastic bands, its muscles. They taped the tubes together, making bendy joints. Then they looped the elastic bands around the tubes. Zuri gently pulled an elastic band, and her puppet’s leg straightened with a soft pop. Bloop pulled another, and its arm lifted. Carefully, they set the puppet upright. It stood tall and proud, not a wobble in sight, as if it had been practising being a person all morning and had only just remembered how. The puppet’s cardboard knees stayed firm, its elastic-band arms held strong, and a faint smell of fresh cardboard hung in the air.

Coach Ellis beamed. “Well done. You’ve given your puppet a skeleton and muscles, just like us. Our bones give us our shape, and our muscles help us move. It is how all living creatures stand strong and play.”

Zuri looked at the puppet, then at her own small hands. Understanding bones and muscles had made such a difference. “What else in the world moves because of bones and muscles?” she wondered.

Bloop’s lights blinked in happy agreement. “Let’s find out together!” he chirped—especially if the next thing that needed standing up was waiting, just a little wobbly, on the science-fair table.
characters: Zuri (careful coder), Bloop (cheerful robot), Ellis (workshop coach)
author: StoryGen Community
